questions.question_stem: A trace of stolen funds ends at three exchange addresses: a deposit address, the hot wallet and a cold wallet. Which one points at a single customer account?
questions.correct_answer: The deposit address, because the exchange makes it for one customer, while the hot and cold wallets pool everyone's coins.
incorrect_answers: The hot wallet, because it pays withdrawals and so is the address that the receiving customer's own account uses most.
The cold wallet, because the exchange assigns each customer a share of the offline funds under a separate address.
All three, because the exchange holds every key and so each address names the same account for the same trace.
questions.explanation: Deposit addresses are created per customer, so a payment into one is a payment into one account. Hot and cold wallets hold pooled (omnibus) coins; naming them says only which exchange.

questions.question_stem: On Ethereum, address X receives ETH, and within an hour sends on almost the same amount to address H, which has received tens of thousands of such forwards. What is X most likely?
questions.correct_answer: A deposit address that the exchange behind H controls, forwarding to its main address and keeping a little for the fee.
incorrect_answers: A mixer contract, because a near-equal amount sent on within hours is how a mixer returns coins to the same sender.
An exchange customer's own wallet, because ordinary users send on almost all of a payment to one regular address.
A hot wallet, because only a hot wallet forwards funds quickly and in nearly full amounts to a second address.
questions.explanation: Three tells mark an Ethereum sweep: nearly the same amount (less the fee), a short wait, and one destination that receives thousands of such forwards. Together they point at a deposit address.

questions.question_stem: An Ethereum deposit address forwards a token deposit in full but forwards an ETH deposit slightly reduced. Why does the token forward lose nothing?
questions.correct_answer: The fee is paid in ETH from another source, because a transaction fee cannot be paid in tokens at all.
incorrect_answers: Tokens carry no transaction fee, because the token contract pays the network on behalf of the sender instead.
Token transfers are settled inside the exchange's books, so the forward on the chain is a free transfer.
The exchange waives the fee on tokens, because a stablecoin transfer is kept at par with its own sender.
questions.explanation: An ETH forward pays its fee out of the amount, so it is slightly smaller. A token forward must be paid for in ETH from another source, so the full token amount moves on.

questions.question_stem: One Bitcoin transaction spends 60 inputs, each funded by a different sender in the last few hours, into two outputs. What does the common-input heuristic correctly tell the analyst?
questions.correct_answer: The 60 inputs share one key holder, the exchange, but the coins belong to many separate customers.
incorrect_answers: The 60 inputs belong to one customer, because the heuristic says that inputs spent together share an owner.
The 60 inputs show the exchange paying 60 withdrawals, since each input matches one customer payment.
The 60 inputs are unrelated, because a heuristic built for single users cannot be applied to a business.
questions.explanation: In a sweep the exchange controls the keys but not the coins: the heuristic correctly links the inputs to the exchange, and wrongly reads as one customer if applied blindly.
questions.lesson_block: On Bitcoin, a sweep gathers many deposits

specific_source.anchor: On Bitcoin, a sweep gathers many deposits

questions.question_stem: A junior analyst merges the 60 inputs of a suspected exchange sweep into a single cluster and labels it as one customer's wallet. What is the correct way to treat the cluster?
questions.correct_answer: Merge the inputs into the exchange's cluster, never into one customer, since they were separate customers' deposits.
incorrect_answers: Keep it as one customer, because the exchange holds the keys for the account of whoever funded each deposit.
Discard the cluster, because any transaction with that many inputs is too noisy to support a link of any kind.
Split it into 60 clusters, one per input, because every deposit was funded by a different customer at the exchange.
questions.explanation: The sweep links the deposit addresses to the exchange's control. It says nothing that joins the senders who funded them, who are many separate customers.

questions.question_stem: Customer A deposits 1 BTC at an exchange. An hour later, 1 BTC leaves the exchange's hot wallet. Can the analyst treat it as A's withdrawal?
questions.correct_answer: No: the hot wallet holds many customers' coins, so only the exchange's own records can link a deposit to a withdrawal.
incorrect_answers: Yes, because a withdrawal of the same amount within hours is how an exchange returns a customer's own deposit.
Yes, if the destination is a new address, because exchanges pay a withdrawal to a fresh address for that customer.
No, because exchanges always delay withdrawals by a day, so an hour-old match must come from another source.
questions.explanation: Withdrawals are paid from a shared pool, and trades and transfers happen in the exchange's ledger. The chain cannot link a deposit to a later withdrawal; the exchange's records can.
questions.lesson_block: Withdrawals come from the pool, not the deposit

specific_source.anchor: Withdrawals come from the pool, not the deposit

questions.question_stem: Exchange withdrawals on Bitcoin often form a peeling chain: one large balance pays a small amount out and sends the rest to change. How should an analyst treat the pattern?
questions.correct_answer: As common for ordinary exchange withdrawals, so on its own it raises a question and does not show wrongdoing.
incorrect_answers: As proof of laundering, because only a person hiding the origin of funds would send change back to themselves.
As the mark of a mixer, because mixers use peeling chains to split a pooled balance into small payouts.
As a sign of a stolen wallet, because a thief empties a balance one small payment at a time to avoid notice.
questions.explanation: Meiklejohn et al. saw peeling chains in the withdrawals of many banks and exchanges. The pattern alone does not distinguish a legitimate pool from a launderer.

questions.question_stem: Addresses A and B both sent funds to deposit address D, which forwards to an address labelled as exchange X. What does the lesson allow the analyst to say?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate confidence that A and B are controlled by one entity, since a deposit address belongs to one account.
incorrect_answers: High confidence that A and B are one entity, because a shared deposit address is proof that the sender is the same.
Nothing, because two senders to a shared deposit address are only linked when they paid at the same time.
Moderate confidence that A and B are the exchange, because a deposit address belongs to the exchange itself.
questions.explanation: One deposit address means one account, so its senders are likely one entity. The heuristic has known false positives, so the reading takes a confidence word and names the label.

specific_source.anchor: Shared deposit addresses link their senders

questions.question_stem: Many addresses send to one exchange address that takes payments for many customers, told apart by a destination tag or memo. What does sharing that address show?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing on its own; a matching tag, memo or muxed address would suggest one account, as an inference.
incorrect_answers: One entity, because the exchange gives each such address to one customer and so every sender is the same.
One exchange, because sharing the address shows that the exchange controls every account that paid into it.
Many entities that cooperate, because a shared address marks a pooled group of customers at the exchange.
questions.explanation: On XRP Ledger and Stellar, one exchange address can serve many customers and the tag or memo names the account. Link senders only when the tag, memo or muxed address matches too.

questions.question_stem: Three senders each paid an address that forwards its full amount to an address labelled as an exchange wallet. The analyst writes Moderate confidence that one entity controls the senders. Why not High?
questions.correct_answer: High needs a second, independent kind of evidence; here the label is unverified, and a forwarder can fake a link.
incorrect_answers: High is used only when the senders were seen together in one block, which a forwarding pattern never shows.
High is reserved for forwards of an exact amount, because rounding in the received sum breaks the link in practice.
Moderate is the lowest word the lesson allows, because any link drawn from a forwarding pattern starts there.
questions.explanation: The lesson gives a forwarding pattern Moderate confidence: one strong line, and an adversary can build a forwarder to fake a link. A confirmed label on the destination strengthens it, and High needs a second, independent kind of evidence. A forwarder that also sends elsewhere would lower it.

questions.question_stem: A trace ends: funds reached Exchange X's hot wallet. Which finding should the analyst write instead?
questions.correct_answer: Name the deposit address and the transaction paying into it, keeping the sweep as proof it is the exchange's.
incorrect_answers: Name the hot wallet, because it is the address a trace lands on and it tells the reader the most about the customer.
Name the cold wallet, because the exchange keeps most of its funds there and so it is where the customer's coins rest.
Name all three exchange addresses, so the reader can see which one pays out the customer's withdrawal.
questions.explanation: A deposit address points at one account; the hot and cold wallets point at the whole exchange. The sweep ties the deposit address to the exchange, and says nothing more about the customer.
questions.lesson_block: Name the deposit, not the sweep

questions.question_stem: A buyer settles a large crypto trade through an OTC desk. Which part of the trade can the analyst see on the chain?
questions.correct_answer: Only the settlement, and only if it goes to an outside wallet; the deal and its price stay off-chain.
incorrect_answers: The whole trade, because a desk posts each order to its address before sending the coins on.
The agreed price, because the desk's transfer amounts are set by the quote and so reveal the terms of the deal.
Nothing at all, because a desk settles every trade in its own books and never pays an outside wallet.
questions.explanation: An OTC desk matches a buyer and a seller off the open order book, so the negotiation is off-chain. Only the settlement, if it leaves the desk for an outside wallet, appears on the chain.

specific_source.anchor: OTC desks trade large amounts off the order book

questions.question_stem: An address gathers many small payments from unrelated senders and then makes a few large transfers to an exchange. How should the analyst read it?
questions.correct_answer: As consistent with an OTC desk that launders, but only a question, since most desks are legitimate ones.
incorrect_answers: As a legitimate OTC desk, because large transfers to an exchange are how every desk settles with its customers.
As a confirmed laundering desk, because gathering small payments into large ones is proof of structuring.
As a mixer, because any address that gathers many senders and pays out in lumps is running a mix.
questions.explanation: Chainalysis describes laundering OTC desks that collect small deposits into wholesale amounts. The aggregation shape raises a question; a merchant or payroll account can look the same.

questions.question_stem: Two P2P trades each lock the crypto in an escrow. One uses a platform's escrow wallet, as Paxful did; the other uses a Bisq 2-of-2 multisig. What differs in who holds the coins?
questions.correct_answer: The platform holds the key and can freeze the escrow and keep records; in the multisig neither trader can do so.
incorrect_answers: Both let the platform freeze the escrow, because each P2P market keeps a copy of the key to settle any dispute.
Neither is frozen by anyone, because the escrow's script locks the coins until the two traders both sign a payout.
The multisig holds records of both traders, because a 2-of-2 script stores each party's name with its public key.
questions.explanation: Paxful controlled the private key to its escrow wallet. In Bisq both traders lock coins in a 2-of-2 multisig, so neither can move them alone, and a dispute goes to a mediator and then arbitration.
questions.lesson_block: P2P markets: two people trade, an escrow holds

specific_source.anchor: P2P markets: two people trade, an escrow holds

questions.question_stem: Which P2P arrangement leaves no company able to freeze the escrowed crypto, and why?
questions.correct_answer: A 2-of-2 multisig, because no company sits in the middle and neither trader alone can move the coins.
incorrect_answers: A platform's escrow wallet, because the key is shared between the two traders and no company can use it.
Both, because a P2P market can never freeze coins that are held on a chain and not in an exchange account.
Neither, because every P2P market keeps a copy of the key and can freeze any trade that is in dispute.
questions.explanation: An exchange can freeze funds, and a platform holds the escrow key. With a 2-of-2 multisig, no company is in the middle, so no one party alone can freeze the coins.

questions.question_stem: Thirty unrelated addresses each send $5,000 to $9,000 of a stablecoin to address Y over two days. Y then sends $220,000 in one transfer to an exchange's deposit address. What does the analyst write?
questions.correct_answer: Low confidence in OTC aggregation, since a merchant or payroll account can look alike; name the exchange deposit.
incorrect_answers: High confidence in OTC laundering, because gathering small deposits into one wholesale transfer is the lesson's pattern.
Moderate confidence in an exchange sweep, because many deposits gathered into one transfer is how a sweep looks.
No reading at all, because the sources the lesson cites do not describe a pattern of this kind on a stablecoin.
questions.explanation: The pattern fits OTC aggregation, but a merchant or payroll account can look the same, so the behavior alone gives low confidence. The exchange deposit is what can be named and followed.
questions.lesson_block: Practice: characterize three patterns

questions.question_stem: On Ethereum, an ETH deposit leaves address X for an exchange's main address in full, with nothing kept back for a fee. Does that rule X out as a deposit address?
questions.correct_answer: No: a contract deposit address forwards automatically, and the sender's transaction pays the fee.
incorrect_answers: Yes: the exchange pays each ETH forward's fee from the deposit, so a full forward means a user.
No: the exchange pays the fee for an ETH forward in tokens, so the ETH itself arrives in full.
No: a full forward means the exchange waited, then paid one fee to forward several deposits.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading explains that the forwarded ETH is often slightly less because the exchange pays the fee, but a smart-contract deposit address forwards automatically and the sending transaction has already paid the fee, so nothing is kept back. Fees cannot be paid in tokens, and waiting for more deposits does not remove the fee.

questions.question_stem: Deposit address D is paid by a mining pool's payout address and by another exchange's hot wallet, and forwards both to exchange X. Should the analyst link those two senders to D's customer?
questions.correct_answer: No: a pool payout or an exchange withdrawal comes from a shared service wallet, not the customer.
incorrect_answers: Yes: every address that pays into one deposit address belongs to the customer behind that account.
Yes: a pool and an exchange that both pay one deposit address are probably run by one operator.
No: a deposit address only links senders that paid it inside the same short forwarding window.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading's heuristic ignores senders that are known exchange addresses or miners: users send straight from one exchange to another, and mining pools pay members' shares directly to deposit addresses. Those senders are shared services paying on the customer's behalf, not the customer's own addresses.

questions.question_stem: The deposit-address heuristic links 4,000 sending addresses into one entity, all through a single deposit address. How should the analyst read that cluster?
questions.correct_answer: As likely wrong: the deposit address may be an unlabelled exchange or service that many people use.
incorrect_answers: As one large entity, since each deposit address is made for one customer however many addresses pay in.
As the exchange itself, since a deposit address and every address that pays into it belong to the exchange.
As one key holder, since many addresses gathered in one place share a key, as in a Bitcoin sweep.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading treats clusters of more than 1,000 addresses as unlikely and drops them, and its Discussion says some very large clusters could come from exchange addresses missing from the label list. The exchange controls the deposit address, but the senders are its customers, and a shared destination is not a shared key.

questions.question_stem: Private address F receives ETH from address A and at once sends the same amount to an exchange's main wallet. F is not a deposit address. What false link could the heuristic draw?
questions.correct_answer: It could treat F as a deposit address and link A with anyone else who paid F, as one entity.
incorrect_answers: It could treat F as the exchange's hot wallet and link every customer of that exchange with A.
It could treat A as a deposit address and then link the exchange's main wallet to F's own owner.
None: a forward that keeps nothing back for any fee is a pattern the heuristic already skips.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading's Limitations show that anyone who forwards a received amount to a known exchange wallet makes their address look like a forwarding deposit address, so the senders to it are pulled into one cluster. An exact forward still counts, because the heuristic allows any difference from zero up to its threshold.
